profile.name: Buffalo dance
profile.tagline: A sacred Plains Native ceremony invoking buffalo spirits for survival, health, and herds.
profile.insight: In 1894, the Buffalo Dance became one of the earliest films featuring Native Americans, capturing a sacred tradition historically shared by the Mandan, Sioux, Cheyenne, Pawnee, and Omaha.
profile.profile: The Buffalo Dance, also known as the Bison Dance, is a traditional festival and ceremony performed by Native American Plains tribes, including the Mandan, Sioux, Cheyenne, Pawnee, and Omaha. Historically timed to coincide with the return of bison herds, the ceremony sought to ensure food abundance, resources, and community well-being. In some societies, such as the Chaui Band of Pawnee, the Buffalo Dance formed part of larger seasonal rituals like the Painting of the Buffalo Skull ceremony or served healing functions. Dancers traditionally wore buffalo and animal skins, moving to ancestral song cycles inherited through tribal lineage.
profile.profile_long:
The Buffalo Dance, or Bison Dance, is a significant ceremonial tradition among North American Plains Natives, including the Mandan, Sioux, Cheyenne, Pawnee, and Omaha tribes. Historically, the ritual was linked to the seasonal return of bison herds. Because the bison was essential to Plains society, providing food, clothing, shelter, and tools, communal dances were performed to ensure the return of the herds and guarantee community survival. Beyond hunting rituals, the Buffalo Dance could also form part of larger spiritual gatherings such as the Sun Dance or serve specialized functions aimed at curing the sick by invoking the spirit of the buffalo.

Technique and visual movement details remain restricted or unrecorded in public historic texts. During early observations, such as Frances Densmore's documentation of Pawnee ceremonies in Oklahoma, dances took place inside sacred structures such as large earth lodges. Dancers and singers held specialized roles; for instance, members of the Buffalo Society participated in sacred preparations like the Painting of the Buffalo Skull ceremony before communal dancing commenced. In 1894, a brief 16-second silent black-and-white film titled 'Buffalo Dance' recorded participants, marking one of the earliest motion pictures featuring Native Americans.

Music for the dance consists of sacred song cycles transmitted through inherited rights. Ethnographic field recordings from the Pawnee tribe preserve old minor-tonality songs led by ceremonial leaders such as Wicita Blain of the Skidi Band. Sung within the earth lodge behind a sacred altar, these songs narrated ancient ancestral events and honored the sacred bond between the tribe and the buffalo spirit.

Because the Buffalo Dance is a sacred and restricted ceremonial tradition among Plains tribes, public observation and participation are strictly governed by tribal protocols. Outsiders must respect the sacred nature of the dance and refrain from imitating ceremonial practices without cultural authority.

sections.origins_and_history: The Buffalo Dance traditionally coincided with the annual return of the buffalo herds among Plains Native groups including the Mandan, Sioux, Cheyenne, Pawnee, and Omaha. The bison was central to Plains Native society, making the dance vital for securing food, resources, and community survival. In 1894, a 16-second silent film recorded people performing the dance, making it one of the earliest films featuring Native Americans.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Detailed dance steps, footwork, and technical movements are not described in sources. Historic documentation notes that a number of men performed the dance wearing buffalo and other animal skins inside structures such as large earth lodges.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music consists of ceremonial songs led by singers who inherited the right to perform them, such as Wicita Blain of the Skidi Band of Pawnee. Recorded songs include ancient compositions in minor tonality describing historical tribal events involving buffalo herds.
sections.costume_and_setting: Participants traditionally wore buffalo and other animal skins. Among the Chaui Band of Pawnee, the dance took place inside a large earth lodge facing east, with a painted buffalo skull resting on a folded blanket in front of an altar opposite the entrance.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The ceremony coincided with the return of buffalo herds, incorporating feasts and spiritual requests for abundance. It also functioned as a section of larger ceremonies like the Sun Dance or as a curing dance calling on the spirit of the buffalo for healing.
sections.notable_figures: Historical figures associated with Pawnee ceremonial performances include Wicita Blain (a blind singer of the Skidi Band who inherited Buffalo dance songs), Mrs. Effie Blain, John Luwak (chief of the Chaui Band), and Stacy Matlock (who managed the Painting the Buffalo Skull ceremony).
sections.regional_variants: The dance was practiced with distinct societal rules across multiple Plains tribes, including the Mandan, Sioux, Cheyenne, Pawnee (Chaui and Skidi bands), and Omaha.
sections.lineage: The songs and ceremonial rights of the Buffalo Dance were passed down through inheritance within specific tribal societies, such as the Buffalo Society of the Pawnee.

profile.sacred_note: The Buffalo Dance is a sacred ritual with spiritual and curing functions; ceremonial details and song rights are restricted to authorized members of tribal societies.

teaching.level_notes: Sacred ceremonial dance; not structured for public instruction.

music_profile.vocal_style: Spiritual ceremonial singing, minor tonality in recorded Pawnee examples.
music_profile.sound_description: Historical Pawnee recordings feature inherited ceremonial songs in a minor tonality led by a lead singer positioned near a sacred altar inside an earth lodge.

movement_profile.formation_and_space: Performed inside a large earth lodge facing an east-facing opening, centered around an altar displaying a painted buffalo skull.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Do not imitate or alter sacred tribal ceremonial rituals without cultural permission and inheritance rights.

episode_brief.title_hook: Spirit of the Bison: The Sacred Buffalo Dance of the Plains
episode_brief.logline: Explore the history, sacred songs, and vital cultural heritage of the Plains Native Buffalo Dance ceremony.
beats: Introduction to the central importance of the bison to Plains Native survival and society.
Archival footage overview of the 1894 silent film 'Buffalo Dance'.
Examination of the Pawnee earth lodge setting and the sacred Painting of the Buffalo Skull ceremony.
Discussion of inherited song traditions led by historical keepers of the songs like Wicita Blain.
Reflection on the enduring spiritual role of the dance in healing and community renewal.

Traditional buffalo and animal skin ceremonial attire.

claims.text: The Buffalo Dance is an annual dance festival of Plains Native groups including the Mandan, Sioux, Cheyenne, Pawnee, and Omaha.
claims.quote: The Buffalo Dance, or Bison Dance, is an annual dance festival of many North American Plains Natives, including the Mandan, Sioux, Cheyenne, Pawnee, and Omaha, among others.

claims.text: The festival coincided with the return of buffalo herds and included a dance with men wearing animal skins.
claims.quote: The festival traditionally coincided with the return of the buffalo herds, and included a feast and a dance with a number of men wearing buffalo and other animal skins.

claims.text: A short silent 1894 film Buffalo Dance was one of the earliest films made featuring Native Americans.
claims.quote: A short, 16-second, black-and-white silent 1894 film Buffalo Dance shows people performing the dance. It is notable for being one of the earliest films made featuring Native Americans.

claims.text: The Buffalo Dance could also refer to a section of larger ceremonies such as the Sun Dance or serve as a curing dance.
claims.quote: The Buffalo Dance can also refer to section of larger ceremonies and dances, such as the Sun Dance. In some societies it was also a dance more associated with curing the ill, calling on the spirit of the buffalo.

claims.text: Wicita Blain of the Skidi Band recorded Buffalo dance songs that were his by right of inheritance.
claims.quote: Mr. Blain recorded songs of the Lance and Buffalo dances which are his by right of inheritance.

claims.text: The ceremony of Painting the Buffalo Skull was held every spring by the Chaui Band of Pawnee in a large earth lodge.
claims.quote: The ceremony of Painting the Buffalo Skull is held every spring by the Chaui Band of Pawnee and is in charge of Mr. Stacy Matlock, a prominent member of that band. The closing events of the ceremony are the Buffalo and Lance dances

claims.text: During the Buffalo dance, the painted buffalo skull lay on a folded blanket in front of the altar opposite the lodge entrance.
claims.quote: during the Buffalo dance the skull, painted a few days previously, lay on a folded blanket in front of the ‘‘altar’’ which was opposite the entrance.
